经过一周繁忙的发射活动，本周全球发射清单预计将进行六次发射，其中包括范登堡发射的 3 次 SpaceX 猎鹰 9 号发射任务、中国的两次发射任务以及南美洲的阿丽亚娜 6 号发射任务。 SpaceX 将为美国太空部队和国家侦察办公室发射有效载荷，而本周的中国任务和阿丽亚娜 6 号任务中至少有一次将发射一批互联网卫星。长征2D |有效载荷未知，将于 11 月 18 日星期三从中国发射，长征 2D (CZ-2D) 预计将于世界标准时间 22:50 从太原卫星发射中心的 9 号发射场 (LC-9) 发射。官方警告通知表明发射轨迹是向南的，但有效载荷及其预定轨道的详细信息要等到发射后才会发布。两级、40.77 米高的 CZ-2D 由上海航天技术研究院 (SAST) 制造。 2D 版本不需要额外的捆绑式助推器。此次飞行将是长征2D的第108次飞行，也是今年的第七次。猎鹰 9 号 | USSF-317 (R-6) SpaceX 将于 11 月 18 日星期三进行本周两次发射中的第一次发射，发射时间为四小时，发射窗口于太平洋标准时间晚上 7:00（世界标准时间周四 03:00）开始。
USSF-317 任务是美国太空军 (USSF) 本周的唯一任务，将从加利福尼亚州范登堡太空部队基地 (VSFB) 的东 4 号航天发射场 (SLC-4E) 发射，向东南飞行，将其机密有效载荷送入低地球轨道 (LEO)。所有系统看起来都很好，天气也有利于升空。猎鹰 9 号发射的 USSF-627 任务即将开始从加利福尼亚州发射推进剂 → https://t.co/IdlZbviZZl pic.twitter.com/fKxyN4DIui — SpaceX (@SpaceX) 2026 年 11 月 12 日助推器 B1100 将支持此次任务，这是自近一年前 11 月 23 日首次支持星链集团 11-30 以来的第十一次飞行， 2025 年。除了 NROL-105 和 USSF-385 之外，助推器之前的八次飞行支持了星链任务。 SpaceX 的西海岸无人机飞船 Of Course I Still Love You 将在 B1100 升空后约 8 分钟着陆时驻扎在地面。猎鹰 9 号是一枚直径 3.9 米、高 70 米的两级火箭。九台 Merlin 1D 发动机为第一级助推器提供动力，而第二级则使用一台真空优化的 Merlin 发动机。猎鹰 9 号和猎鹰重型火箭是第一批实现定期重复使用的轨道火箭，其中一枚猎鹰助推器已飞行 37 次。飞行后，两个有效载荷整流罩也被回收并重复使用。长征8A | SatNet LEO Group 本周第二次中国发射计划于 11 月 11 日星期五举行。
世界标准时间 20 日 11:00，在中国文昌航天发射场的商业 LC-1 发射台上发射。长征 8A (CZ-8A) 将携带 9 颗通信卫星进入近地轨道，这些卫星由 SatNet 拥有并由中国卫星网络集团运营。 CZ-8A火箭有两个直径3.35米的级，总高度为50.54 m。第一级由两个捆绑式液体燃料助推器辅助。此次飞行将是 CZ-8A 的第 13 次飞行，也是 2026 年的第七次飞行。 NROL-136 SpaceX 本周的第二次猎鹰 9 号任务定于 11 月 21 日星期六太平洋标准时间凌晨 4:30（世界标准时间 12:30）发射，同样是从加州 VSFB 的 SLC-4E 发射。 NROL-136 任务将携带未知数量的有效载荷进入近地轨道，供国家侦察办公室 (NRO) 的增殖建筑星座使用，该星座由 Space 建造

【原文 English Original】
Following a week of busy launch activity, the worldwide launch manifest is set to see six launches this week, with three SpaceX Falcon 9 missions from Vandenberg, two Chinese missions, and an Ariane 6 mission from South America. SpaceX will launch payloads for the United States Space Force and the National Reconnaissance Office, while at least one of this week’s Chinese missions and the Ariane 6 will launch a batch of internet satellites. Chang Zheng 2D | Unknown Payload Wednesday, Nov. 18, will see a launch from China, with a Chang Zheng 2D (CZ-2D) expected to launch from Launch Complex 9 (LC-9) at the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center at 22:50 UTC. Official warning notices indicate a southerly launch trajectory, but details of the payload and its intended orbit will not be released until after launch. The two-stage, 40.77-m-tall CZ-2D is manufactured by the Shanghai Academy of Spaceflight Technology (SAST). The 2D variant requires no additional strap-on boosters. This flight will mark the 108th CZ-2D to fly, the seventh of this year. Falcon 9 | USSF-317 (R-6) SpaceX’s first of two launches this week comes on Wednesday, Nov. 18, at the start of a four-hour launch window that opens at 7:00 PM PST (03:00 UTC on Thursday). The only mission for the United States Space Force (USSF) this week, the USSF-317 mission will launch from Space Launch Complex 4 East (SLC-4E) at Vandenberg Space Force Base (VSFB) in California, flying southeast to place its classified payload into low-Earth orbit (LEO). All systems are looking good, and weather is favorable for liftoff. Propellant load is about to begin for Falcon 9’s launch of the USSF-627 mission from California → https://t.co/IdlZbviZZl pic.twitter.com/fKxyN4DIui — SpaceX (@SpaceX) November 12, 2026 Booster B1100 will support this mission, marking its eleventh flight since first supporting Starlink Group 11-30 nearly a year ago on Nov. 23, 2025. Eight of the booster’s previous flights supported Starlink missions, in addition to flying NROL-105 and USSF-385. SpaceX’s west coast droneship, Of Course I Still Love You, will be stationed downrange for B1100’s landing approximately eight minutes after liftoff. Falcon 9 is a 3.9-m-diameter, 70-m-tall two-stage rocket. Nine Merlin 1D engines power the first-stage booster, while the second stage uses a single vacuum-optimized Merlin engine. Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy were the first orbital rockets to achieve regular re-use, with one Falcon booster having flown 37 flights. The two payload fairings are also recovered and reused after flight. Chang Zheng 8A | SatNet LEO Group The second Chinese launch of the week is scheduled for Friday, Nov. 20, at 11:00 UTC from the Commercial LC-1 pad at the Wenchang Space Launch Site in China. A Chang Zheng 8A (CZ-8A) will carry nine communications satellites into LEO, with the satellites owned by SatNet and operated by the China Satellite Network Group. The CZ-8A rocket features two 3.35-m-diameter stages, with a total height of 50.54 m. The first stage is assisted by two strap-on liquid-fuelled boosters. This flight will mark the 13th overall CZ-8A flight, the seventh of 2026. Falcon 9 | NROL-136 SpaceX’s second Falcon 9 mission of the week is scheduled to launch on Saturday, Nov. 21, at 4:30 AM PST (12:30 UTC), again from SLC-4E at VSFB in California. The NROL-136 mission will carry an unknown number of payloads into LEO for the National Reconnaissance Office’s (NRO) Proliferated Architecture constellation, built by SpaceX and Northrop Grumman. The booster supporting this mission will be B1097, flying for the 14th time. This booster first flew on Sept. 3, 2025, and has previously flown eight Starlink missions, as well as NROL-172, Transporter 17, Sentinel-6B, Twilight (Pandora & Others), and USSF-259. Following stage separation, B1097 will conduct a return-to-launch-site landing at Landing Zone 4 (LZ-4), located directly next to SLC-4E. Ariane 64 | Amazon Leo (LE-04) Amazon is continuing to put together its constellation of Leo satellites and will add another 36 on Monday, Nov. 23, at 10:12 UTC aboard an Ariane 64. The rocket will launch from Ensemble de Lancement Ariane 4 (ELA-4) at the Guiana Space Centre in French Guiana, with the launch window lasting five hours and 27 minutes. Ariane 64 will follow a northeastern trajectory, delivering 22,000 kg of Leo satellites into LEO. Ariane 64 is a 62-m-tall, 5.4-m-diameter, expendable two-stage rocket built by the ArianeGroup on behalf of the European Space Agency. Both stages are powered by liquid hydrogen and oxygen-fuelled engines. The 64 variant of the basic Ariane 6 utilizes four P129 strap-on solid rocket boosters to provide additional lift-off thrust. This will be the fifth Ariane 6 mission of 2026. Watch the full replay of #VA269 . Relive Ariane 6's successful mission carrying 36 Amazon Leo satellites into orbit. First flight with P160C boosters Heaviest Ariane payload ever #LaunchingAmbitions #Ariane6 #VA269 @Amazonleo @ArianeGroup @esa @CNES @EuropeSpacePort pic.twitter.com/YLxW60wAo1 — Arianespace (@Arianespace) June 17, 2026 Falcon 9 | USSF-266 (TH-3) Closing out the week, a Falcon 9 launch is currently scheduled for Monday, Nov. 23, at 8:04 AM PST (16:04 UTC) — the third this week from SLC-4E at VSFB. The classified USSF-266 mission has a four-hour launch window extending to 12:04 PM PST (20:04 UTC). Falcon 9 will fly due south, indicating a polar orbit for the payload. While the payload is classified, the launch trajectory and other factors suggest that this may be an additional batch of satellites for the USSF’s Space-Based Airborne Moving Target Indicator (SB-AMTI) program. These are based on the SpaceX Starshield satellite bus. The Falcon 9 booster supporting this flight will be B1081, making its 29th flight. B1081 first flew on Aug. 26, 2023, and flew four missions from SpaceX’s Florida launch sites before moving to Vandenberg for Transporter 10, where it has operated since then. The booster will land atop Of Course I Still Love You , stationed approximately 640 km downrange in the Pacific Ocean. If the current schedule holds, this will mark the 122nd Falcon 9 flight of 2026, and the 273rd orbital launch attempt worldwide in 2026. (Lead Image: Falcon 9 launches into the Florida morning skies. Credit: Julia Bergeron for NSF) The post Launch Preview: Ariane 6 to launch Amazon satellites, Falcon 9 to launch government missions appeared first on NASASpaceFlight.com .

整理经济动力产业：分析研究和政策建议选集|书籍和编辑卷| 2026 年 11 月 16 日 | ITIF跳到内容
整理经济动力产业：分析研究和政策建议选集
中国主导战略重要产业的系统性运动如何威胁美国的技术领先地位、经济实力和国家安全，以及美国政策制定者应该采取什么措施。
信息技术与创新基金会 (ITIF) 进行了为期 18 个月的研究，探讨中国霸道的产业战略如何威胁美国的技术领先地位、经济实力和国家安全。 ITIF 的研究得出的结论是，美国政策制定者必须从根本上改变该国的科技工业经济体系，以防止美国在为 21 世纪国家实力提供基础的关键先进贸易部门行业中屈服于中国。 ITIF 将这些行业称为“国民经济动力行业”。
这项研究工作于 2025 年 11 月至 2026 年 11 月期间产生了一系列 19 份政策报告。
该系列的第一份报告全面概述了中国正在发动的技术经济贸易战，以牺牲美国及其西方盟友的利益来主导这些行业。
第二组九份报告包括对美国工业表现与中国在国民经济实力行业方面的定量和定性分析。
第三组共九份报告，为美国政策制定者提供了近 200 条具体建议，以重组政府并动员起来应对与中国的技术经济贸易战。
这些报告可以连续提供，也可以作为选集提供：
随后是概述报告的执行摘要以及 ITIF 政策建议索引。
中国正在系统性地主导先进产业，从而在 21 世纪增强国家实力，美国面临着生存挑战。与美国历史上的任何竞争对手不同，中国将拥有 14 亿人口的大陆经济规模与明确致力于实现对西方民主世界的技术经济优势的马克思列宁主义政治体系结合起来。这不是市场经济体之间的正常经济竞争，而是一场精心策划的、长达数十年的战略运动，旨在取代美国的工业能力、削弱盟国，并从根本上重塑中共领导下的全球秩序。
其中的利害关系超越了经济范畴。今天的国家实力取决于本报告所称的“国家电力工业”的实力，这些部门涵盖纯粹的国防生产、军事和商业应用中使用的军民两用技术，以及支持更广泛工业公域的赋能产业。其中包括半导体、航空航天、生物制药、电信设备、先进化学品、精密机械、机器人、人工智能（AI）系统以及其他数十个领域，在这些领域，企业实力减弱或受到致命伤害将赋予中国对美国及其盟国的危险影响力，并削弱美国的国防生产能力。
按照目前的发展轨迹，中国很可能很快就会在国家电力行业积累比美国大得多的能力。
本次比赛的对手是 bac

【原文 English Original】
Marshaling Economic Power Industries: An Anthology of Analytical Research and Policy Recommendations | Books & Edited Volumes | Nov 16, 2026 | ITIFSkip to content
Marshaling Economic Power Industries: An Anthology of Analytical Research and Policy Recommendations
How China’s systematic campaign to dominate strategically important industries threatens America’s technological leadership, economic strength, and national security—and what U.S. policymakers should do about it.
The Information Technology and Innovation Foundation (ITIF) has conducted an 18-month research effort examining how China’s domineering industrial strategy threatens U.S. technological leadership, economic strength, and national security. ITIF’s research concludes that U.S. policymakers must fundamentally transform the country’s techno-industrial economic system to prevent America from becoming subservient to China in a critical group of advanced, traded-sector industries that provide the foundation for national power in the 21st century. ITIF calls these industries “national economic power industries.”
This research effort produced a series of 19 policy reports from November 2025 through November 2026.
The first report in the series provides a comprehensive overview of the unfolding techno-economic-trade war that China is waging to dominate these industries at the expense of the United States and its allies in the West.
A second group of nine reports includes quantitative and qualitative analyses of U.S. industrial performance versus China in national economic power industries.
A third group of nine reports offers nearly 200 specific recommendations for U.S. policymakers to reorganize government and mobilize for the techno-economic-trade war with China.
The reports are available both serially and as an anthology:
An executive summary of the overview report follows, along with an index of ITIF’s policy recommendations.
The United States faces an existential challenge in China’s systematic campaign to dominate the advanced industries that enable national power in the 21st century. Unlike any competitor in American history, China combines the continental scale of a 1.4-billion-person economy with a Marxist-Leninist political system explicitly committed to achieving techno-economic supremacy over the Western democratic world. This is not normal economic competition between market economies—it is a carefully orchestrated, multi-decade strategic campaign to displace U.S. industrial capabilities, weaken allied nations, and fundamentally reshape the global order under CCP leadership.
The stakes transcend economics. National power today depends on strength in what this report terms “national power industries”—a spectrum of sectors spanning pure defense production, dual-use technologies employed in both military and commercial applications, and enabling industries that support the broader industrial commons. These include semiconductors, aerospace, biopharmaceuticals, telecommunications equipment, advanced chemicals, precision machinery, robotics, artificial intelligence (AI) systems, and dozens of other sectors in which weakened or fatally injured firms would grant China dangerous leverage over the United States and its allies, as well as weaken U.S. defense production capabilities.
On its current trajectory, it is likely that China will soon amass significantly greater capabilities than the United States will in national power industries.
This competition occurs against a backdrop of American policy failure. For over two decades, U.S. leaders across both parties have operated under the assumption that China was becoming a “normal” market economy that would gradually liberalize politically and economically. That assumption has proven catastrophically wrong. China today is more authoritarian, more aggressive internationally, and more committed to state-directed capitalism than at any point since Mao’s death.
On its current trajectory, it is likely that China will soon amass significantly greater capabilities than the United States will in national power industries. With those greater capabilities will come geostrategic hegemony over the West, unless the United States forestalls that outcome by adopting a new, transformative national power industry strategy that goes beyond a mere competitiveness or national innovation strategy. This is not a war that the United States and allies can win in the sense of significantly weakening or retarding the growth of China’s own national power industries. The only way Chinese attacks will end is if China becomes a free, democratic country. But the United States and allies can avoid defeat—keeping their national power industries relatively strong—by working together and adopting national power industry strategies.
Understanding the Chinese Communist Party’s True Objectives
Perhaps the most damning evidence of Chinese intentions comes from internal Communist Party documents and speeches intended for party members rather than foreign audiences. As China scholar Daniel Tobin has documented, these reveal a regime explicitly committed to Marxist-Leninist global ambitions that go far beyond merely moving up the value chain and growing its economy.
Xi Jinping has repeatedly framed China’s rise in ideological terms, stating that “scientific socialism is full of vitality in 21st century China” and that China offers “a new option for other countries and nations who want to speed up their development while preserving their independence.” In a 2013 speech to senior party officials, Xi declared that “the viewpoint of historical materialism that capitalism is doomed to failure and socialism will prevail” remains valid, and that China must “seize the initiative, win the competitive edge, and secure our future” in a “long-term cooperation and rivalry between the two social systems.”
Documents from the party’s 20th Congress state that China’s success has “significantly shifted the worldwide historical evolution of the contest between the two different ideologies and social systems of socialism and capitalism in a way that favors socialism.” Chinese leaders explicitly describe their work as part of a “great struggle” and “systems contest with Western capitalist democracy,” using terminology that leaves no ambiguity about their intentions.
On technology and industry specifically, party documents are equally explicit. The minister of Science and Technology wrote in the People’s Daily that “the scientific and technological revolution and the contest between major powers are intertwined; the high-tech field has become the forefront and main battlefield of international competition.” Another official commentary stated: “To a certain extent, those who gain access to the Internet will gain the world. Core technology is an important weapon for the country.”
China’s Made in China 2025 plan, while officially downplayed after international backlash, clearly articulates the goal: “Building an internationally competitive manufacturing industry is the only way China can enhance its comprehensive national strength, ensure national security, and build itself into a world power.” The plan calls for China to “seize the commanding heights of a new round of competition in the manufacturing industry” and achieve innovation leadership “ranking first globally.”
The CCP follows a predictable playbook across industry after industry.
Leading Chinese scholar Lu Yongxiang stated in 2024 that “by 2035, ‘Made in China’ will surpass the United States and become the global leader,” noting this would thrust the world into a “new era”—explicitly referencing an era of Chinese dominance. These are not the words of a nation seeking merely to “catch up” or achieve “legitimate development.” They are the explicit articulation of a campaign for global advanced industrial hegemony.
China’s actions match its rhetoric. The CCP follows a predictable playbook across industry after industry. First, attract foreign investment by promising market access. Second, coerce technology transfer through joint venture requirements and other mechanisms—pressure the U.S. Trade Representative has characterized as “particularly intense.” Third, support domestic firms in copying and incorporating foreign technology while building indigenous capabilities through programs such as the 2006 Medium- and Long-term Program for Science and Technology Development, which identified 402 core technologies to master.
Fourth, carve out and protect the Chinese market for Chinese firms, excluding foreign competitors once domestic champions can reasonably serve the entire Chinese market. Fifth, provide massive subsidies—estimated at minimum 1.73 percent of Chinese gross domestic product (GDP) annually, or over $400 billion per year, though actual figures are likely far higher accounting for provincial and local support. Finally, support Chinese firms “going out” to capture global market share, particularly in developing nations through Belt and Road Initiative investments exceeding $1 trillion. These dwarf the minimal industrial subsidies the U.S. government (USG) provides.
The scale of Chinese subsidies dwarfs anything in Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) nations. A German institute found that in 2022, 99 percent of listed Chinese firms received direct government subsidies, with electric vehicle (EV) maker BYD alone receiving over $3.7 billion. Chinese industrial subsidies were 4.5 times greater than U.S. subsidies as a share of GDP. Combined with a chronically undervalued currency, suppressed domestic consumption, and closed markets, these subsidies have enabled Chinese firms to sell below cost for years or decades, systematically destroying foreign competitors’ market positions.
This is not to say that all Chinese efforts or innovation are win-lose. If China invents a cure for Alzheimer’s, the world benefits (assuming the United States or its allies would not also do so). But this would also reduce U.S. (and allied) strength in the pharmaceutical industry.
Overall, the policy debate about China is largely dominated by international relations scholars and experts, not business or industrial strategy experts. The former are aware of the global competition for leadership in advanced industries, but they largely see it as subservient to overall foreign policy considerations and goals. Moreover, few understand the operation of advanced industries, the nature of the competition, or the importance of barriers to entry and reentry. As such, the prevailing narratives largely ignore techno-economic and trade war implications and the implications for U.S. power.
Current U.S. thinking about China coalesces around three main strategic approaches, all of which are inadequate to the challenge.
The first camp, still influential in much of the U.S. foreign policy establishment, prioritizes maintaining cooperative relations with China, even in the face of CCP behavior that harms U.S. national power industry capabilities. These experts argue that China’s growth benefits global prosperity, that Chinese cooperation is essential for addressing climate change and other global challenges, and that confrontation risks becoming a catastrophic conflict.
A 2019 open letter signed by over 100 prominent scholars claimed that “we do not believe Beijing is an economic enemy or an existential national security threat” and argued that “the fear that Beijing will replace the United States as the global leader is exaggerated.”
This camp consistently minimizes Chinese malfeasance while emphasizing supposed benefits of engagement. They cite Chinese economic growth as driving global prosperity (ignoring that China’s persistent trade surpluses actually reduce GDP elsewhere). In arguing that cooperation is needed on issues such as climate change, pandemic response, and AI governance, they gloss over the question of why the United States should be the supplicant when China has equal or greater interest in addressing these challenges.
Their fundamental error is treating China as a partner rather than a strategic competitor. Engagers assume that continued dialogue and economic ties will moderate China’s behavior, when two decades of evidence proves otherwise. They prioritize the process of engagement over the substance of outcomes, accepting Chinese predatory practices as the price of maintaining access and conversation.
The Deniers: Wait for China’s Collapse or Assume Inherent U.S. Superiority
A second camp acknowledges China’s rise but counsels patience, predicting that internal contradictions will lead to Chinese economic stagnation or political crisis. These analysts point to demographic decline, the housing bubble, government debt, and the inefficiencies of state capitalism as harbingers of inevitable Chinese failure. To be sure, many advance the well-trodden prescriptions such as improved K-12 education, more high-skill immigration, smarter regulation, and more government spending on science. But they will not go so far as to support a national power industry strategy.
This “Peak China” thesis is seductive because it requires no painful U.S. policy changes. If China is destined to collapse under its own weight, the United States need only wait and maintain its existing approaches to the economy, trade, and national security. Proponents cite any negative Chinese economic news as evidence that their predictions are materializing, while ignoring continued Chinese gains in technological capabilities and global market share of advanced industries.
The fatal flaw is mistaking China for the Soviet Union. Unlike Soviet command economics, Chinese state capitalism has proven remarkably effective at generating growth and technological advancement. The CCP studied why the Soviet Union failed and adopted fundamentally different economic management—allowing market forces to operate within state-directed strategic frameworks rather than attempting to centrally plan everything.
Moreover, even if China faces economic headwinds from demographics or debt, these business-cycle challenges do not negate its structural advantages in the techno-economic competition. Chinese firms will continue benefiting from massive subsidies, protected markets, and patient capital regardless of GDP growth rates. Waiting for China to self-destruct while Chinese companies dismantle Western industries one after another is a prescription for defeat.
The Innovationists: Technology Will Save Us
The third camp acknowledges the challenge China presents but argues that American innovation superiority will enable the United States to prevail. These “dynamists” focus on deregulation, immigration reform, scientific research funding, and nurturing entrepreneurship—particularly in cutting-edge fields such as AI, quantum computing, and synthetic biology.
This view holds that the United States need not defend legacy industries because American innovators will create entirely new sectors and the United States will lead them. Why fight over solar panels or EVs when we can dominate AI and quantum? The prescription is to boost science funding, reduce regulatory barriers, import more STEM (science, technology, engineering, and math) talent, and trust that Silicon Valley-style innovation will deliver victory.
The problems with this strategy are multiple. First, with a few exceptions (e.g., AI), it is industry-agnostic—there is no guarantee that market-driven innovation will produce capabilities in sectors that matter most for national power. Second, the United States has repeatedly lost production of technologies it invented, from televisions to solar panels to batteries, as other nations have commercialized American discoveries. Innovation alone does not ensure domestic production or competitive strength.
Third, advanced defense systems increasingly rely on commercial technologies (spin-on rather than spin-off), making a strategy that abandons commercial sectors to China while hoping to maintain defense-only production unrealistic and prohibitively expensive. Fourth, the “industrial commons”—the ecosystem of suppliers, skilled workers, and manufacturing capabilities—erodes when industries disappear, making future innovation harder. Intel founder Andy Grove’s warning resonates: “Abandoning today’s ‘commodity’ manufacturing can lock you out of tomorrow’s emerging industry.”
Finally, China is not ceding emerging technologies. Chinese firms are competitive or leading in AI (see Alibaba, Baidu, and DeepSeek), quantum communications, commercial space, robotics, and biotechnology. The notion that the United States can retreat to “higher ground” in emerging tech while China dominates established industries ignores that Chinese firms are aggressively pursuing both.
Why Current U.S. Economic Policy Frameworks Fail
The deeper problem is that dominant U.S. economic doctrines are fundamentally mismatched to the era of national power industry competition.
The reigning paradigm in U.S. economic policymaking—which critics call “neoliberalism”—treats all industries as equivalent. Financial services and semiconductor fabrication are no different; both simply respond to market signals. The goal is to maximize consumer welfare through efficient resource allocation, which markets achieve better than governments do.
In this framework, Chinese subsidies (including low labor costs and lax environmental regulations) are gifts to American consumers (lower prices!), not strategic attacks. Trade deficits reflect American prosperity (we’re rich enough to buy foreign goods!), not industrial weakness. Offshoring production to China demonstrates smart capital allocation by U.S. firms seeking higher returns, not a national security vulnerability.
The reigning paradigm in U.S. economic policymaking—which critics call “neoliberalism”—treats all industries as equivalent.
Consumer welfare economics has no concept of strategic industries or national power. Its proponents argue that “countries don’t compete, only companies do” and that concerns about industrial structure reflect economically illiterate protectionism. The Peterson Institute epitomizes this view, arguing that U.S.-China trade is “clearly win-win” and that “Chinese companies have a right to compete with U.S. companies and succeed in any sector, including in high-tech.”
This doctrine might have been adequate when America faced no serious techno-economic competitor; it is catastrophically inadequate against China’s state capitalist predation. Markets have no inherent reason to preserve semiconductor fabrication, aerospace, or pharmaceutical production domestically. They are equally happy producing legal services, retail, and hospitality, none of which enable national power.
But the reality of this techno-economic and trade attack fundamentally undercuts the foundation of consumer welfare economics and exposes its inability to address the current challenge. If national power is the ultimate goal, not consumer welfare, then this doctrine fails, at least in guiding the share of the economy composed of national economic power industries. If a nation’s industrial mix is critical, then a doctrine that gives equal weight to potato chips and computer chips fails.
The ascendant alternative on the Left is equally unsuited to the challenge. Neo–New Dealism focuses on redistribution, social justice, and worker welfare overgrowth and competitiveness. Its industrial policy priorities are human services (childcare, eldercare), climate-focused sectors (renewable energy), and breaking up large corporations through aggressive antitrust.
While rhetorically supporting “industrial policy,” progressives’ actual agenda—drug price controls, restricting intellectual property (IP), mandating labor standards that limit automation, attacking profitable corporations as exploitative—systematically weakens the large advanced-technology firms that must serve as national champions against Chinese competitors.
Moreover, neo–New Dealism’s massive social spending agenda would consume the fiscal resources needed for strategic industrial investment. Its anticorporate ideology and deep suspicion of business-government collaboration make the public-private partnerships required for an effective national power industry strategy politically toxic.
The reality of the CCP’s techno-economic and trade war on the West undercuts the foundations of neo–New Deal progressivism. If the United States is in an existential contest for global power, then boosting taxes and regulations on business is especially ill-advised, as are the neo-Brandeisian campaign to destroy large corporations and separate unrestrained demands from organized labor. Progressive advocates know this quite well, which is why they go to any end to deny that China is even a competitor.
What’s Required: National Power Industry Strategy
The United States needs a fundamentally new framework: a national power industry strategy. This approach recognizes the following:
Industries differ fundamentally in strategic importance. Semiconductors and furniture are not equivalent. Some sectors—defense, dual-use, and enabling—are critical to national power and must be prioritized even at short-term economic cost.
Markets are indifferent to national power. Unregulated market forces will not automatically preserve strategic capabilities. Government must actively shape industrial structure through strategy, not just generic competitiveness or innovation policies.
China is a strategic competitor, not a normal trading partner. Chinese mercantilism requires defensive measures (restricting imports produced unfairly) and offensive support (strengthening domestic champions in national power industries) that violate free-market and progressive orthodoxies.
Production matters as much as innovation. The United States cannot rely on inventing technologies that China then produces. Manufacturing capabilities, supply chain resilience, and industrial commons must be preserved domestically in strategic sectors.
Long-term strategic positioning trumps short-term efficiency. Maintaining redundant capacity, subsidizing strategic industries, and accepting higher consumer prices are necessary costs of not losing the techno-economic war.
This requires jettisoning the deeply held view that governments should not “pick winners.” Markets might optimize GDP growth, but only by happenstance will this generate needed national power industry capabilities. Policymakers must embrace strategic industry selection and support, drawing on business strategy frameworks rather than consumer welfare economics.
The political economy obstacles to a national power industry strategy are severe. U.S. business leaders, shaped by decades of financial capitalism prioritizing quarterly returns and shareholder value, distrust government involvement and focus myopically on firm-level profitability rather than systemic strength. Unlike their predecessors from the 1940s–1970s who saw themselves as corporate statesmen with responsibilities to the broader capitalist system, today’s executives view government industrial policy as either incompetent interference or the thin edge of socialist control.
Labor unions pursue short-term wage gains that often undermine firms’ long-term global competitiveness because they are unable to escape the prisoner’s dilemma of aggressive bargaining today leading to job losses to less-constrained Chinese rivals tomorrow.
Conservative organizations reflexively oppose the government activism required for industrial strategy, while progressive organizations reflexively oppose supporting corporations. Neither party’s dominant coalition supports the combination of strong state capacity and empowered corporate champions that a national power industry strategy requires.
Perhaps most critically, the USG itself lacks the analytical capacity, institutional structures, and personnel with expertise to formulate and execute sophisticated industrial strategy. Unlike China, where officials study industrial policy as a discipline and spend careers mastering sectoral dynamics, U.S. policymakers typically have backgrounds in law or generalist economics divorced from operational understanding of specific industries and technologies.
The United States requires political, policy, and institutional transformation comparable to previous pivots after the War of 1812, the Civil War, and World War II. In all three cases, war provided the spur to overcome inertia and interest group resistance. We certainly hope it will not take a physical war to achieve similar transformation today. Either way, the organizing principle of economic policy must shift from maximizing consumer welfare or spurring social justice to ensuring that the United States maintains superior capabilities in national power industries relative to China. The simplest measures of this are the share of these industries’ global output that is produced in the United States and the share of U.S. production that occurs in allied nations. Related measures are the technological sophistication of U.S. products and services in national power industries compared with those of Chinese competitors.
The United States requires political, policy, and institutional transformation comparable to previous pivots after the War of 1812, the Civil War, and World War II.
This demands classifying industries by strategic importance, developing sophisticated strategies for priority sectors informed by business strategy principles rather than economics, restricting unfairly traded Chinese goods’ access to allied markets, substantially increasing public and private investment in strategic sectors (on the order of $100 billion per year in tax incentives and direct expenditures for at least a decade), coordinating with allies to present unified responses, and building government institutional capacity for industrial strategy.
The costs will be significant: Implementing a national power industry strategy will bring higher prices for certain consumer goods, increased government spending, greater fiscal discipline elsewhere, and reduced returns for some investors as capital is channeled toward strategic rather than merely profitable uses. But the alternative is worse: a future in which Chinese dominance of advanced industries leaves the United States dependent on an adversary for critical technologies, unable to defend its interests or protect its allies, and relegated to second-tier status in a China-dominated world order.
History shows that America can make fundamental pivots when circumstances demand. Whether it can do so absent the shock of military conflict—which might come too late, after critical capabilities are already lost—remains the defining question of our era. The window for effective action is narrowing. Chinese positions in industry after industry are becoming entrenched, protected by economies of scale, learning curves, network effects, and the enormous barriers to reentry that characterize advanced manufacturing. The reality is that once advanced industry capabilities are lost, they are extremely difficult to resurrect.
The choice facing America is stark and unavoidable: Fundamentally reform techno-economic policy now by embracing the uncomfortable truth that some industries matter far more than others—and by recognizing that preserving them requires active government strategy—or accept a managed decline into second-tier status while China’s techno-economic dominance translates into geopolitical supremacy. There is no third option, no magical innovation breakthrough that will solve the problem without hard choices and real sacrifices.
The United States remains far stronger than any declining power in history. Its advantages in innovation ecosystems, allied networks, capital markets, universities, and democratic legitimacy provide a foundation for successful competition if properly mobilized. But time is not on America’s side. Every industry lost makes recovery harder; every year of Chinese industrial expansion shifts the balance further; every failure to act because it violates free-market or progressive orthodoxies surrenders ground that cannot be regained. The techno-economic war with China is the central challenge of the 21st century. America’s response will determine not just its own future but the future of the liberal democratic world.

如今，对于美国避免与中国进行代价高昂且危险的军备竞赛的能力，华盛顿盛行悲观主义——几乎是宿命论。政策制定者指出，中国对台湾日益咄咄逼人的政策、大规模的军备建设以及拒绝采取某些军备控制措施，证明北京已经接受了这种竞赛的必然性，甚至正在追求一场竞赛。由于担心强调敌对大国之间爆发战争可能性的知识框架，许多美国领导人和分析人士认为，美国别无选择，只能武装自己。但这种想法有可能成为一种自我实现的预言。主要危险在于，无节制的军备竞赛会增加台湾战争甚至灾难性核交锋的可能性。
但对于避免军备竞赛的悲观情绪是错误的。尤其是核军备竞赛还不是板上钉钉的事——美国确实有机会遏制核军备竞赛。避免核军备竞赛需要采取比华盛顿最近青睐的双管齐下更广泛的方法：建立美国的核威慑力量，并寻求通过限制贸易和技术转让来迫使北京做出让步。相反，美国领导人应该超越传统的威慑（这种威慑因其基于威胁的方法往往会引发军备竞争而显得不足），并努力通过相互缓和和妥协的过程来建立更根本的战略稳定。中国可能会愿意相互缓和局势：它在核问题上有着温和的传统，而且最终，中国领导人不希望因台湾问题爆发战争。
最近有迹象表明，即使是经常吹嘘自己厌恶妥协的美国总统唐纳德·特朗普也看到了接触的价值。在今年两次美中双边峰会之后，他在十月份建议，十一月份在深圳与中国领导人习近平和俄罗斯总统普京举行的三边会议应重点讨论“无核化”。但华盛顿必须更加坚定地反对军备竞赛，包括改变对台湾的支持，并将中国纳入全球军控领导地位。只有华盛顿继续相信这一点，与中国的核军备竞赛才变得不可避免。

Today, pessimism—almost fatalism—reigns in Washington about the United States’ ability to avoid a costly and dangerous arms race with China. Policymakers point to China’s increasingly aggressive policies toward Taiwan, its massive military buildup, and its resistance to engaging in some arms control measures as evidence that Beijing has accepted the inevitability of such a race or is even pursuing one. Worried by intellectual frameworks that emphasize the likelihood of war between rival great powers, many U.S. leaders and analysts see little choice but for the United States to arm itself, too. But this thinking risks becoming a self-fulling prophecy. The major danger is that an unrestrained arms race increases the likelihood of war over Taiwan or even of a catastrophic nuclear exchange.
But the pessimism about averting an arms race is misplaced. A nuclear arms race, in particular, is not a foregone conclusion—and the United States has real opportunities to curb one. Avoiding a nuclear arms race will require a broader approach than the two-pronged one Washington has recently favored: building up U.S. nuclear deterrence and seeking to force concessions from Beijing by imposing restrictions on trade and technology transfers. American leaders should instead look beyond traditional deterrence, which falls short because its threat-based approach tends to provoke competition over arms, and strive to establish a more fundamental strategic stability through a process of reciprocal de-escalation and compromise. China is likely to be amenable to reciprocal de-escalation: it has a long tradition of moderation in nuclear matters and, ultimately, Chinese leaders do not want a war over Taiwan.
There are recent signs that even U.S. President Donald Trump, who has often boasted about his distaste for compromise, sees the value of engagement. After two U.S.-Chinese bilateral summits this year, in October he suggested that his November trilateral meeting in Shenzhen with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin should focus on “denuclearization.” But Washington will have to become much more consistent in its rejection of an arms race, including by modifying its support for Taiwan and incorporating China into global arms control leadership. A nuclear arms race with China becomes inevitable only if Washington continues to believe it is.
China is undoubtedly pursuing a military buildup, including investments in nuclear weapons. Between 2020 and 2025, China doubled the number of its nuclear warheads, from 300 to 600—a startling increase, although its arsenal remains small compared with the United States’ approximately 3,700 warheads. In 2021, researchers at the Federation of American Scientists announced that China was constructing 350 new nuclear missile silos in three vast sites in Xinjiang and Gansu provinces. Beijing is also pursuing substantial qualitative upgrades to its nuclear weapons, a push it showcased at an October 2025 military parade that unveiled a new sea-launched ballistic missile, two new kinds of intercontinental ballistic missiles, a new air-launched hypersonic missile, and a new long-range hypersonic cruise missile.
Then, this July, the Chinese navy tested a submarine-launched long-range ballistic missile that could carry nuclear weapons. This significant new capability will allow China to launch long-range nuclear strikes that can reach the United States from protected waters near its own coastline rather than having to sail out into the Pacific. A recent editorial in a leading Chinese foreign affairs newspaper took the candid yet disturbing step of explicitly linking China’s rapid nuclear buildup to its desire to exert sovereignty over Taiwan. “The great cause of national reunification,” it asserted, “must rest on a solid, realistic foundation. That foundation is, first and foremost, hard power.” Although such overt nuclear saber rattling remains rare, the link between Beijing’s nuclear forces and the Taiwan issue stretches back over three decades and is also supported by the scholar Tong Zhao’s detailed analysis of China’s nuclear buildup in Foreign Affairs in May.
As China builds up its military, the perception that it is on a collision course with the United States over Taiwan—one that inevitably includes the risk of nuclear escalation—has become widespread in Washington. Taiwan, of course, appears to be an obvious flash point. The United States has long committed itself informally to defending the island while China seeks to unify with it, by force if necessary. In October, Army General Ronald Clark, the head of the U.S. Pacific Command, affirmed that his forces are actively readying for a Chinese invasion of Taiwan that could come as early as 2027.
The Biden administration and both Trump administrations made some attempts to engage China over arms control and nuclear risk reduction. Trump proposed trilateral arms control talks that would include Russia, whereas the Biden administration pursued bilateral talks with China on strategic stability and nuclear risk reduction. But both presidents gave up after China consistently rejected engaging in sustained talks on nuclear matters. Beijing’s stance is that it has a small nuclear arsenal compared with the United States and Russia and that it is important to first establish trust and mutual reassurance about core interests.
Beyond China’s resistance to arms control, theories about power that are trendy in Washington reinforce the collision course mentality. Numerous realist scholars argue that a U.S.-Chinese rivalry and even a great-power war may be structurally difficult to avoid. The political scientist Graham Allison captured this pessimism in his influential 2017 book, Destined for War, which argued that a so-called Thucydides trap—when a rapidly rising power challenges the position of the dominant power, yielding war—would doom the United States and China to conflict.
China hawks, such as Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby, increasingly advocate an aggressive focus on “preparing for World War III” with China as a way to avoid it. In a July New York Times interview, Colby argued that the United States must “deny” China “the ability to seize and hold the key territory” of Taiwan, by enhancing U.S. deterrence with a massive military buildup. The next month, speaking at a military conference, Colby specified that such a buildup ought to put a greater emphasis on tactical nuclear weapons and the ability to fight a so-called limited nuclear war. The enemy, Colby said, has “got to believe there’s some sense in which we would use” nuclear weapons. Toward this end, the United States is building a new intercontinental ballistic missile, a new air-launched cruise missile, and new nuclear-armed submarines and bombers, and accelerating the ambitious Golden Dome homeland missile defense project. Unlike earlier U.S. missile defenses, which were designed to intercept limited strikes by so called rogue states such as Iran and North Korea, the Golden Dome is intended to defend against massive Chinese or Russian attacks. But the prospect of losing its ability to retaliate against a U.S. first strike only gives Beijing more incentive to expand its nuclear arsenal.
Such a nuclear-heavy approach only prevents a war with China if nuclear deterrence succeeds. That puts a lot of eggs in the deterrence basket. And recent wars suggest that nuclear deterrence is becoming less effective. Russia’s nuclear threats have not coerced Ukraine into halting its strikes deep into Russian territory. Iran has proved willing to launch strikes against nuclear-armed Israel as well as U.S. bases and allies in the Middle East. What is most ominous, in May 2025, India and Pakistan crossed previous redlines and attacked each other’s homelands, something that mutual nuclear deterrence was supposed to prevent. Even if neither the United States nor China want nuclear war, a China determined to unify with Taiwan may not be intimidated by U.S. nuclear threats.
A recent study by Brown University’s Costs of War program found that the United States has already spent more than $3.4 trillion on its militarized rivalry with China over the last decade. Sustaining or ramping up this spending—which encompasses new warships, aircraft, long-range missiles, drones, base upgrades, forward deployments, large military exercises, research and development, and new nuclear weapons—is infeasible in an era of ballooning national debt and expanding domestic needs.
One of the tragedies of an arms race is that neither party may actually want to pursue one. Despite its current arms buildup, Beijing has a long record of moderation in military and nuclear matters. For many decades, it has maintained a minimal nuclear deterrent and a no-first-use policy, and it did not use major military force to achieve strategic goals. Although it has long had access to the relevant technologies, China appears not to have produced or deployed tactical nuclear weapons. Chinese diplomats played a substantial role in coaxing Iran to accept the Obama administration’s 2015 nuclear deal and supported the UN’s relatively stringent sanctions on North Korea. And in the fall of 2022, according to then Secretary of State Antony Blinken and reporting by the Financial Times, China likely intervened diplomatically with the Kremlin to help stop Russia from using nuclear weapons in Ukraine. More broadly, China has embraced international law when it comes to war, playing a constructive role, for example, in removing chemical weapons from Syria in 2013.
The United States has already spent more than $3.4 trillion on its militarized rivalry with China.
Beijing’s inclination toward restraint has not disappeared completely, even as it upgrades its military. In November 2023, U.S. President Joe Biden and Xi agreed to renew lines of communication between their countries’ militaries that had been severed after U.S. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taiwan the previous year. A year later, the two leaders affirmed that humans, not AI, must control the decision to use nuclear weapons. And in late 2025, Beijing released a white paper emphatically reiterating its support for nuclear arms control and has moved toward more transparency by publishing more information, including in English, about its military upgrades.
Chinese leaders clearly do not want a war over Taiwan. Publicly, they repeatedly emphasize that their goal is “peaceful unification” and “winning without fighting,” invoking the Chinese strategist Sun-tzu. Beijing’s longtime “one country, two systems” policy toward Taiwan—which would bring the island under Chinese sovereignty while allowing it substantial autonomy—leaves room for a negotiated solution. Last year, in an important analysis of China’s strategic ambitions, the scholars David Kang, Jackie Wong, and Zenobia Chan examined 12,000 articles and hundreds of speeches by Xi to argue that Beijing prioritizes regime stability and internal development over displacing the United States as a global military hegemon. Although China’s major, unannounced exercises around Taiwan earlier this month may constitute an exception, overall, Chinese military exercises near Taiwan over the last five years are consistent with this interpretation: many have reacted to perceived provocations, illustrate only medium-scale capabilities, and have generally had a performative quality, accompanied by extensive press coverage.
There is still an opening for the United States and China to de-escalate. To achieve strategic stability, the two countries will need to make a concerted effort to defuse their security dilemma—the dynamic in which each side perceives the other’s defensive measures as aggressive. First, U.S. and Chinese leaders need to revive superpower summitry. Biden held only three face-to-face meetings with Xi on the sidelines of regional economic meetings. Although the May 2026 Beijing summit between Trump and Xi yielded no major breakthroughs, the meeting did improve the two leaders’ personal relationship; today, U.S.-Chinese tensions are lower than they were between 2021 and 2025. This progress suggests the great value of holding a regular, annual, multiday bilateral summit with a significant focus on nuclear arms control. Such meetings would give expert working groups time to methodically develop measures to reduce the risk of conflict. Just as important, the summits need to be long enough to leave room for unscripted conversations. At their first summit, in Geneva in November 1985, U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev famously broke away from anxious bureaucrats and advisers for an impromptu walk—an encounter that helped establish a more constructive relationship.
The United States must also take concrete steps to reduce the chance of escalation in the Taiwan Strait. Above all, it should adhere more consistently to its “one China” policy—its position that Beijing is the sole legal government of China. More consistency would include limiting U.S. legislators’ trips to the island and downgrading U.S.-Taiwanese defense relations by, for example, holding meetings less frequently and at lower diplomatic levels. Washington should remind key allies such as Japan to proceed cautiously in terms of their rhetoric and military deployments. Such a restraint-oriented strategy would make it clear to Taiwan that independence is off the table, encouraging it to take a more accommodating approach that would lower the temperature with Beijing. If Washington were to agree to common-sense limitations on arms sales to Taiwan—such as refusing to sell Taiwan the surface-to-surface ballistic Army Tactical Missile System (ATACMS), which can reach across the strait to the Chinese mainland—Beijing would likely reciprocate by scaling back its military exercises and related military deployments around the island. There are real incentives for Beijing to de-escalate. Doing so could improve relations with neighbors such as Japan, free up focus for domestic priorities, lower military spending, and limit the chance of war.
The Pentagon needs to demonstrate Washington’s intent to avoid war over Taiwan by gradually decreasing U.S. warship transits through the Taiwan Strait. Even more important, Washington should also substantially reduce U.S. military deployments in the Luzon Strait between Taiwan and the Philippines and around Japan’s Ryukyu Islands. Such deployments only exacerbate the security dilemma.
Above all, Washington should adhere consistently to its “one China” policy.
Exhibiting restraint does not mean the United States would be giving Taiwan away. The United States can continue to provide Taiwan with defensive arms (such as missile interceptors, artillery, drones, and mines) and harden U.S. bases in the region to provide stabilizing deterrence. But even if U.S. leaders publicly abjure direct military intervention to defend Taiwan—a rational step that would lower the risk of nuclear war—China will prefer negotiating with Taipei on the island’s autonomy over a bloody military showdown with Taiwanese forces. For their part, Taiwan’s leaders will likely accommodate themselves to limited self-governance under Chinese overall sovereignty. In the end, China’s main goal is to get Taiwan out of the U.S. sphere of influence. Chinese leaders’ major fear is not so much Taiwanese autonomy as the prospect of the island serving as a U.S. forward base—in Chinese parlance, “using Taiwan to contain China.”
Another important step would be to seek a multilateral pledge by all nuclear-armed states to employ nuclear weapons only in retaliation against a nuclear attack. Such a policy would reduce the risk of miscalculation during a crisis. China has long embraced such a no-first-use policy, but U.S. leaders have traditionally opposed it, believing that it might expose U.S. allies to conventional attack. The U.S. nuclear deterrent for allies, however, increasingly lacks credibility because the costs of starting a nuclear war would vastly outweigh the benefits. And after the collapse of traditional nuclear arms control, a mutual no-first-use policy offers a promising area of common ground between the United States and China. It would reinforce the existing no-first-use policies of China and India and implicitly acknowledge their leadership in the area of nuclear restraint, a virtue when newer nuclear states are chafing under the old Cold War superpowers’ dominance of arms control. This approach could even entice Beijing into a wider, more comprehensive process of bilateral or multilateral nuclear arms control.
Beyond these three major initiatives, the United States and China should sign an agreement to notify each other about their ballistic missile tests. Washington could also consider giving Beijing a larger role in nonproliferation efforts, for instance by affording China leadership roles in negotiations and inspection regimes in future nonproliferation arrangements. The U.S. arms control agenda with China should focus not only on offensive nuclear systems but also on missile defenses and tactical nuclear weapons, as well as AI technologies. And it would help if the United States evolved its own nuclear posture in the direction of restraint by reducing its warheads, warfighting capabilities, and alert posture.
Ultimately, the United States needs to get serious about reining in an arms race with China before its perception that one is apace becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. The two countries have a mutual interest in restraint. If Washington continues to overlook Beijing’s incentives to compromise—and the real signs that it is willing to do so—an arms race that, as of now, is mostly putative will become a reality. And a catastrophic war that could have been avoided could indeed become inevitable.

title: Optimizely hack infected CNN, Fox News, BBC, Salesforce sites with malware
zh_title: 优化利用恶意软件攻击受感染的 CNN、福克斯新闻、BBC、Salesforce 网站
summary: Optimizely 黑客入侵了带有恶意软件的 CNN、Fox News、BBC、Salesforce 网站 Optimizely 黑客入侵了带有恶意软件的 CNN、Fox News、BBC、Salesforce 网站 Optimizely 黑客入侵了带有恶意软件的 CNN、Fox News、BBC、Salesforce 网站 针对 Optimizely 的供应链攻击导致恶意 JavaScript 被加载到众多流行网站上，包括 Zoom、CNN、Fox News、BBC、Salesforce 和 GitLab，使访问者暴露于旨在窃取加密货币和支付信息并利用 iOS 设备漏洞的脚本。 Optimizely 是一个数字体验和实验平台
content:
优化利用恶意软件攻击受感染的 CNN、福克斯新闻、BBC、Salesforce 网站
优化利用恶意软件攻击受感染的 CNN、福克斯新闻、BBC、Salesforce 网站
优化利用恶意软件攻击受感染的 CNN、福克斯新闻、BBC、Salesforce 网站
针对 Optimizely 的供应链攻击导致恶意 JavaScript 被加载到许多热门网站上，包括 Zoom、CNN、福克斯新闻、BBC、Salesforce 和 GitLab，使访问者暴露于旨在窃取加密货币和支付信息并利用 iOS 设备漏洞的脚本。
Optimizely 是一个数字体验和实验平台，组织可以使用它来测试和个性化其网站，并将其 JavaScript 文件加载到客户的网页中以提供此功能。
该公司向 BleepingComputer 证实，攻击者利用其实验帐户注册流程中的漏洞将恶意 JavaScript 注入客户项目中，导致使用该平台的网站加载恶意软件。
Optimizely 告诉 BleepingComputer：“今天早些时候，Optimizely 发现了一起安全事件，其中未经授权的一方利用了实验帐户注册流程中的漏洞。”
“他们用它向一些客户项目添加恶意 JavaScript。我们已经阻止了对易受攻击路径的访问并部署了修复程序。我们已经从受影响的项目中删除了注入的代码。我们还结束了活动会话，撤销了令牌，并重置了受影响用户帐户的访问权限。最后，我们阻止了在 Cloudflare 中交付的任何代码。
“我们正在继续调查并将在 status.optimizely.com 上发布任何相关更新。我们已通知所有受影响的客户。”
该攻击首先由安全研究员 Scott Helme 发现，他周一报告说，他的团队在分析该平台使用的 1,611 个脚本后，发现了属于 178 个组织的 188 个受感染的 Optimizely JavaScript 文件。
BleepingComputer 独立确认，恶意脚本已通过 urlscan.io 记录的扫描加载或试图加载到许多受影响的网站上，包括 Zoom、KLM、GitLab、BBC、Scheels、CNN、American Girl、ManageBuilding、Smartsheet、Stamps.com 和 Salesforce。
其他受影响的网站包括 Fox News、Mutual of Omaha、American Eagle、Air France、Change.org、Optimizely、HSBC Insurance、Bitly、IG 和 UNICEF USA。
Salesforce 确认正在调查对其某些网站上使用的 Optimizely 脚本的恶意修改。
“作为预防措施，Salesforce 正在确认 Optimizely 脚本在预览和生产实例中被禁用。我们将继续调查，如果我们发现未经授权的数据访问，我们将立即通知受影响的客户，”Salesforce 告诉 BleepingComputer。
BleepingComputer 分析了修改后的 Optimizely JavaScript 文件的副本，并确认攻击者已注入旨在从 https://1688360[.]cc/track.js 加载其他恶意脚本的代码。
注入的代码使用多种方法来加载有效负载，其中一些文件直接引用恶意URL，而其他文件则使用Base64编码和JavaScript的atob()函数来解码URL。
Helme 还发现了一种变体，如果远程脚本被阻止，该变体可以执行嵌入的恶意代码副本。

对恶意 track.js 文件的分析揭示了多种功能，Helme 也在他的调查中记录了这些功能：
加密货币

【原文 English Original】
Optimizely hack infected CNN, Fox News, BBC, Salesforce sites with malware
Optimizely hack infected CNN, Fox News, BBC, Salesforce sites with malware
Optimizely hack infected CNN, Fox News, BBC, Salesforce sites with malware
A supply chain attack targeting Optimizely has led to malicious JavaScript being loaded on numerous popular websites, including Zoom, CNN, Fox News, BBC, Salesforce, and GitLab, exposing visitors to scripts designed to steal cryptocurrency and payment information and exploit vulnerabilities in iOS devices.
Optimizely is a digital experience and experimentation platform used by organizations to test and personalize their websites, with its JavaScript files loaded into customers' webpages to deliver this functionality.
The company confirmed to BleepingComputer that attackers exploited a vulnerability in its Experimentation account signup flow to inject malicious JavaScript into customer projects, causing websites using the platform to load malware.
"Earlier today, Optimizely identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the Experimentation account signup flow," Optimizely told BleepingComputer.
"They used it to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects. We have blocked access to the vulnerable path and deployed a fix. We have removed the injected code from affected projects. We have also ended active sessions, revoked tokens, and reset access for affected user accounts. Finally, we have blocked any code from being delivered in Cloudflare.
"We are continuing to investigate and will publish any relevant updates at status.optimizely.com. We have notified all affected customers."
The attack was first uncovered by security researcher Scott Helme, who reported Monday that his team identified 188 infected Optimizely JavaScript files belonging to 178 organizations after analyzing 1,611 scripts used by the platform.
BleepingComputer independently confirmed that the malicious script loaded, or attempted to load, on numerous affected websites using scans recorded by urlscan.io, including Zoom, KLM, GitLab, BBC, Scheels, CNN, American Girl, ManageBuilding, Smartsheet, Stamps.com, and Salesforce.
Other affected websites include Fox News, Mutual of Omaha, American Eagle, Air France, Change.org, Optimizely, HSBC Insurance, Bitly, IG, and UNICEF USA.
Salesforce confirmed it is investigating the malicious modifications to Optimizely scripts used on some of its websites.
"As a precaution, Salesforce is confirming Optimizely scripts are disabled across preview and production instances. We continue to investigate and will notify affected customers without undue delay if we identify unauthorized access to their data," Salesforce told BleepingComputer.
BleepingComputer analyzed copies of the modified Optimizely JavaScript files and confirmed that attackers had injected code designed to load an additional malicious script from https://1688360[.]cc/track.js.
The injected code used several methods to load the payload, with some files referencing the malicious URL directly, while others used Base64 encoding and JavaScript's atob() function to decode the URL.
Helme also identified a variation that could execute an embedded copy of the malicious code if the remote script was blocked.
Malicious JavaScript injected into an Optimizely script loaded by Fox News
An analysis of the malicious track.js file revealed several capabilities, which Helme also documented in his investigation:
Cryptocurrency hijacking: Monitors webpages for cryptocurrency wallet addresses and replaces them with attacker-controlled addresses to steal transfers.
Payment card skimming: Searches for credit card numbers, expiration dates, and security codes entered into webpages, and attempts to transmit the captured information to https://1688360[.]cc/card.php.
iOS exploit delivery: Loads additional malicious JavaScript targeting iPhones and iPads. Helme identified these secondary payloads as the Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits, which target different iOS versions.
The malicious script also contains functionality to collect browser cookies, webpage URLs, and screenshots, which can be transmitted to the attackers.
Helme's investigation found that cryptocurrency wallets embedded in the `track.js` script had received approximately $7,000 in transactions as of November 16. However, some wallets were active before the attack, making it difficult to determine how much cryptocurrency was stolen during the campaign.
Below are the cryptocurrency wallet addresses identified by BleepingComputer in the malicious JavaScript, along with the transaction activity observed as of November 16.

Helme reported that Optimizely's cleanup had reduced the number of infected scripts, with only one of the 188 previously compromised files still containing malicious code as of 21:52 UTC on November 16.
His investigation showed the earliest observed Optimizely script injection in the early morning of November 16, although it remains unclear how long the vulnerability had been present or how many website visitors were exposed to the malware.
Visitors who accessed affected websites on November 16 should review any cryptocurrency transfers made during that time to ensure the destination wallet addresses were not replaced by the malware.
Anyone who entered payment card information should monitor their credit card accounts for unauthorized transactions and contact their card issuer if they notice suspicious activity.
iPhone and iPad users who visited affected websites should ensure their devices are running the latest available iOS or iPadOS updates, as the attack also delivered exploit kits targeting vulnerabilities in older versions.
Overall, users should also watch for suspicious account activity, particularly if they were logged into sensitive services while visiting affected websites.
